change.describe: commit 108f295 of t3code-fork against its parent (d536b05)
change.title: fix(server): bound slow-client event buffers (#9715)
change.author: Theo Browne

findings.title: Every live event is JSON.stringify'd on the event loop just to be measured
findings.body: `serializedSize` stringifies each raw event once (cached per object in the WeakMap). `replace` (line 109) also stringifies every projected or shell output item, and those are fresh objects per subscription, so the WeakMap doesn't help them. For tool events, each event is therefore serialized twice before the WS layer serializes it a third time. A 4 MB payload (the size the new server test uses) costs a multi-megabyte stringify on the PubSub consumer fiber, synchronously. AGENTS.md lists websocket/CPU cost as a standing audit area. A cheaper size estimate could work, for example a field-length sum, or the encoded size if the RPC layer already computes it. If exact bytes are wanted, the stringify cost on the streaming hot path should at least be acknowledged in the doc comment.

findings.title: Buffer overflow is reported to clients as OrchestrationGetSnapshotError
findings.body: The overflow reuses `OrchestrationGetSnapshotError`. `subscribeThread` already uses the same error type for "Thread … was not found" (ws.ts:1678). Can the client-runtime consumers (for example `state/threads.ts` and the shell sync) tell "buffer full, resubscribe from your cursor" apart from a hard snapshot failure, or do they only match on `_tag`? I did not find a client path that handles this error specially. If they treat it as terminal or as a deleted thread, a slow client would stop syncing instead of resuming. The message text asks the client to resume, but nothing typed carries that.

findings.title: `closed` and `usage` are exposed only for tests
findings.body: Nothing in ws.ts reads `closed` or `usage` from the coalescer. `LiveStreamBudget` exports `closed`, `usage` and `release` in the same way, and ws.ts uses only `retain`, `replace`, `deliver`, `failed` and `release`. Test-only observability is reasonable here because the tests wait on these in place of sleeps. If you keep them, a one-line comment that they are for tests would stop others copying them into production paths.

contracts.action: subscribeThread live buffering now runs through ThreadLiveEventCoalescer.offerAll with a per-subscription budget (1000 items / 8 MiB), and delivery goes through budget.deliver
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous path: unbounded input queue plus a processing fiber, with offerAndWait/takeAll used to place the synchronized marker (removed in this diff).
contracts.before_after: Before, offer enqueued and a separate fiber coalesced. Now offerAll coalesces inline under a mutex. The marker is retained, flushed after pending updates, and offered into the same output queue via Stream.unwrap, so ordering is queue order. The unwrap is evaluated when concat reaches it, i.e. after catch-up or snapshot, matching the old fromEffect timing.
contracts.visible_effect: Events reach the client in the same order as before. A subscriber that doesn't ACK past 1000 retained items or 8 MiB gets OrchestrationGetSnapshotError and the PubSub consumer is detached immediately (server test at server.test.ts:8096).
contracts.failure_mode: On overflow, budget.failed fires. The forked close() clears pending/output and fails the queue, and the PubSub consumer is raced against `failed`. deliver's pull fails on its next `check`, so the stream fails once the held ACK is released. In-flight items stay charged until the scope closes. If overflow happens during catch-up or snapshot, deliver has not started yet, and the failure surfaces when the concat reaches the live stream.

contracts.action: subscribeShell live buffer is now budgeted: retain on the PubSub producer, replace in groupedWithin coalescing, deliver around the whole output
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous path: Queue.unbounded plus coalesceShellLiveStream. The coalescing logic is unchanged but now swaps retained items through budget.replace.
contracts.before_after: Before, the buffer grew without bound while the snapshot loaded or the client lagged. Now it fails the subscription at 1000 raw items or 8 MiB. Nothing drains the buffer between attach and the first pull of the live stream, which only happens after the snapshot chunk is ACKed.
contracts.visible_effect: A client that falls behind during snapshot load, or one that stalls on ACK, is disconnected with OrchestrationGetSnapshotError and must resubscribe. The test at server.test.ts:8256 shows it recovering through a fresh snapshot.
contracts.failure_mode: retain/replace are synchronous (Effect.suspend, no awaits), so producer and consumer fibers cannot interleave inside a budget update. closeLiveBuffer is guarded by liveBufferClosed. Under sustained heavy output across all threads, a client could overflow again right after resubscribing, because every thread's raw events are charged to the shell subscription.

contracts.action: Two overlapping calls on the same budget or coalescer (concurrent retain/replace/close, window flush vs offerAll)
contracts.equivalent_path: Old code serialized everything through a single input queue and processing fiber; new code uses a Semaphore mutex plus synchronous budget operations.
contracts.before_after: offerAll, the window flush fiber and close() all take mutex.withPermits(1), so pendingUpdates, windowFiber and the closed flag are only touched under the lock. The budget's retain/replace/release do no awaits between the read of retained state and the write, so A and B cannot lose each other's charge. cancelWindow interrupts a window fiber that may be waiting on the mutex; that wait is interruptible, so there's no deadlock.
contracts.visible_effect: No dropped or reordered events found.
contracts.failure_mode: If flushPending overflows, pendingUpdates is left intact. close() then releases it under the mutex after the offering fiber exits.

summary: The change bounds per-subscription live buffers at 1000 items or 8 MiB, counting the batch awaiting an RPC ACK. Overflow fails the stream with OrchestrationGetSnapshotError and detaches the PubSub consumer without waiting for the ACK. I read the diff for races, cleanup order and ACK gating and found no defect. Retain/replace are synchronous, the coalescer is serialized by a mutex, and the failure and close paths are guarded. The new tests are deterministic and use latches in place of sleeps. I raised three consider-level points. First, every live event is JSON.stringify'd synchronously just to be measured. Second, overflow reuses the snapshot error type, and I couldn't confirm the clients tell it apart from a hard failure. Third, `closed` and `usage` are exposed only for tests. One tradeoff is left for a person to decide: how well the shell subscription, which charges every thread's raw events to one budget, copes with a long snapshot load or bursty output.
